 "id": "Q66",
 "sourceFile": "Time for a Diferent Approach to Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries- Educate and Create Realistic Expectations.pdf",
 "decision": "EXCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "(b) Opinion piece: published under the 'CURRENT OPINION' heading in Sports Medicine, in which the authors 'propose an individualised approach' to ACL management, with no original methods and no structured review of evidence.",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title in text 'Time for a Different Approach to Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries: Educate and Create Realistic Expectations' (Zadro and Pappas, Sports Medicine) matches the filename, apart from the misspelling 'Diferent' and non-breaking spaces in the filename.",
 "confidence": "medium",
 "studyDesign": "Narrative Review",
 "primaryDomain": "Rehabilitation & Return to Sport",
 "domains": [
  "Rehabilitation & Return to Sport",
  "Sports Medicine & Injury"
 ],
 "audiences": [
  "Rehabilitation",
  "Sports Medicine",
  "Athletic Training"
 ],
 "sports": [
  "Mixed / General Sport"
 ],
 "populations": [
  "Injured Athletes",
  "Mixed / Unspecified"
 ],
 "evidenceSummary": "Article in the Current Opinion section of Sports Medicine (Zadro and Pappas, 2018) with no described search method. It draws on cited trials and cohort studies to argue for educating patients on the natural history of ACL injury, offering conservative management as a first-line option, and guiding rehabilitation by a return-to-sport timeframe of at least 9 months after surgery.",
 "screeningLimitations": "This is an opinion article without a described search, so the evidence is selected by the authors and rests heavily on a few trials. The 9-month minimum is a clinical recommendation rather than a validated decision rule, and the authors say the research supporting patient education is limited.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff may read this as proof that non-operative care is better for everyone, but the authors say non-operative management is not the golden ticket and that the choice should follow shared decision making.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2018,
  "citation": "Zadro JR, Pappas E. Time for a Different Approach to Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries: Educate and Create Realistic Expectations. Sports Med. 2018.",
  "doi": "10.1007/s40279-018-0995-0",
  "abstract": "The authors propose an individualised approach to ACL injury that shifts care toward conservative management with surgery as needed. They argue for educating patients on the natural history of ACL injury and for rehabilitation guided by a return-to-sport timeframe of at least 9 months after surgery.",
  "tldr": "Patients should be told that surgery and intensive rehabilitation do not guarantee a good result, and that conservative care was not inferior in the cited trial. Patients who have surgery should aim for no earlier than 9 months to return to sport, with gradual increases in training load.",
  "methods": "Opinion article with no described search method. It draws on cited studies, including a randomised trial of 121 patients comparing early reconstruction with conservative care and trials comparing home with supervised rehabilitation.",
  "findings": "The cited five-year trial found no between-group differences in knee symptoms, function, quality of life, sports participation or radiographic osteoarthritis between early reconstruction and conservative care. Cited trials found home exercise was not inferior to supervised physiotherapy after reconstruction. The article notes only about 65% of patients return to pre-injury sport after reconstruction, nearly one in four have a further ACL injury, and patients rarely pass return-to-sport criteria before 9 months.",
  "limitations": "Without a described search, the choice of evidence cannot be checked, and several key claims rest on single studies. The authors note there is no research comparing supervised with home rehabilitation after non-operative management, and that research on patient education is still needed.",
  "practicalImplications": "Clinicians should explain the natural history of ACL injury and the option of conservative care before surgery. Home exercise can be offered without assuming it is inferior, and the level of supervision should follow patient preference and resources.",
  "athleteDev": "Suggests that training load should rise gradually during ACL rehabilitation, with strength and functional performance built before return to pivoting sport. The load-ratio argument is drawn from general injury-risk research rather than ACL studies, so treat it as guidance.",
  "rtp": "Supports a return-to-sport timeframe of no less than 9 months after surgery, with strength and functional criteria such as limb symmetry above 90% as the main gate. For non-operative care the authors suggest criteria rather than a fixed time, but they do not give a validated return-to-sport test."
 },
 "verification": {
  "status": "DECISION_CHANGED",
  "changes": [
   "decision: INCLUDE -> EXCLUDE (b); text is headed 'CURRENT OPINION' and states 'In this article, we propose an individualised approach', with no search or structured review",
   "exclusionReason: added",
   "paper.methods/screeningLimitations: 'Narrative article' / 'opinion-style' -> 'Opinion article'",
   "paper.findings: 'most do not pass return-to-sport criteria before 9 months' -> source wording ('patients rarely pass RTS criteria following ACLR before 9 months')"
  ],
  "residualConcerns": "Borderline genre call. Excluded for consistency with verified Q94 (also a Sports Medicine 'CURRENT OPINION', excluded under (b)). The piece is evidence-heavy (about 45 references) and carries usable ACL return-to-sport guidance (9-month floor, LSI above 90%), so the operator may prefer to treat it as a narrative review and INCLUDE. Taxonomy and paper fields were kept and checked against the text so an override needs no rework.",
  "spotCheckPriority": "high"
 }
}
